_intro.method: Method: the exact dots of each picture were read from the page itself (one dot per number, 1 to 500,000). On the 23 layouts with a grid, every straight line in 24 directions was cut into stretches where the numbers follow one polynomial (linear or quadratic), and every stretch of 30 or more numbers was compared with the Bateman–Horn prediction, which says how many primes a polynomial should give from the small primes that can divide it. The round layouts and the walks were measured with their own tools. The Mersenne exponents were tested against 300 random sets of the same size and growth.
_intro.answer: Every pattern is explained. The bright lines are polynomials that small primes cannot divide, the dark lines polynomials that a small prime always divides, and the Bateman–Horn formula predicts each line’s number of primes: across 1.6 million stretches the deviations are what chance gives. The space-filling curves have no straight lines at all. The Mersenne exponents line up nowhere more than random sets of the same growth do.

rows.seen: Vertical stripes: light and dark columns.
rows.explained: A column holds the numbers with one remainder mod 708 = 2²·3·59. Columns whose remainder shares a factor with 708 hold no primes (dark); the other φ(708) = 232 hold all of them, each about 708/232 = 3.05 times as many as random numbers (Dirichlet’s theorem).

snake.seen: Stripes of the rows mixed in pairs; short slanted streaks.
snake.explained: Every second row is reversed, so a column alternates between two remainders c and 709 − c; the bright lines are arithmetic progressions, predicted by Dirichlet’s theorem.

honeycomb.explained: The honeycomb keeps a column’s remainder every second row, so its straight lines are progressions with steps 1416 = 2·708 and 2·708 ± 1; bright where the step and start share no factor.

crt.seen: Vertical stripes, no long lines across.
crt.explained: Column = n mod 690, row = n mod 727. Columns sharing a factor with 690 = 2·3·5·23 hold no primes except 2, 3, 5 and 23 themselves; only 176 columns hold the rest. Neighbouring cells are far apart in n, so straight lines are short and carry no structure beyond that.

bands512.seen: Fine vertical stripes and diagonals within each band.
bands512.explained: Width 512 = 2⁹: a column is n mod 512, so every prime is in an odd column. The brightest diagonals are progressions with step 510 = 512 − 2, about 510/φ(510) = 3.98 times random.

binblocks.seen: Each block striped; a staircase of blocks.
binblocks.explained: In every block the column is n mod the block width (a power of 2), so all primes share the odd columns; bright diagonals are progressions with step 510 as in the bands.

spiral.seen: Diagonal streaks of primes, some long.
spiral.explained: Every straight line of the Ulam spiral is a quadratic 4t² + bt + c. The brightest diagonal is Euler’s m² + m + 41 again (here with m even), 6.65 times random; dark diagonals are quadratics that factor, like the odd squares.

ulam41.seen: One long bright diagonal through the centre.
ulam41.explained: Euler’s m² + m + 41: 434 primes among the 707 numbers on it, 6.6 times random, because no prime up to 37 ever divides one of its values.

hex.seen: Bright and dark lines in three directions.
hex.explained: The straight lines are quadratics 3s² + bs + c; the brightest is 3s² + 3s + 23, which no prime up to 19 can divide.

diamond.explained: The lines are quadratics; the brightest is 2s² − 199, also the brightest line of the triangles: no prime up to 31 divides it (constant 7.32).

shells.seen: Bright lines fanning from the corner.
shells.explained: The straight lines are quadratics; the brightest is Euler’s m² + m + 41 (as s² + s + 41 shifted), dark ones include the squares down the left column.

klauber.seen: Vertical bright and dark lines below the apex.
klauber.explained: Each vertical line is r² − r + c; the brightest is Euler’s polynomial, the darkest the squares and r² − 1 at the right edge.

legendre.seen: Bright and dark slanted lines; rows of squares at the bottom.
legendre.explained: The lines are quadratics in k; the brightest is Euler’s polynomial, the bottom row the squares (no primes).

tree.seen: Bright vertical and slanted lines; two dark lines on the right edge.
tree.explained: Every straight line of the tree is a quadratic. The brightest is 2s² − 199: no prime up to 31 (nor 41, 47, 53, 59) ever divides it, so its Bateman–Horn constant 7.32 beats even Euler’s 6.65: 183 primes where random numbers give 24. The right edge holds r(r + 1)/2 and (r − 1)(r + 2)/2, which factor.

floyd.explained: The same quadratics as the tree; the brightest is 2s² − 199.

diag.seen: As the tree, tilted into a corner.
diag.explained: The same quadratics; the brightest is 2s² − 199, the top rows the triangular numbers.

zigzag.seen: As the diagonals, with alternating direction.
zigzag.explained: The same quadratics as the tree; the brightest is 2s² − 199.

sierpinski.explained: Here light means an odd binomial coefficient C(r − 1, j), not a prime: by Lucas’ theorem that is when j and r − 1 − j share no binary 1. The rows that are entirely odd are r − 1 = 2^k − 1, the Mersenne numbers. The prime lines are those of the tree.

hilbert.explained: The curve keeps neighbours together and has no straight runs: not one stretch of 30 numbers lies on a polynomial line. The texture is the primes’ own irregularity.

moore.explained: The same: no straight polynomial runs.

peano.seen: Noise in a base-3 pattern of blocks.
peano.explained: No straight polynomial runs; within blocks the ternary order shows.

morton.seen: Every second column empty of primes; noise otherwise.
morton.explained: The last bit of n − 1 is the column’s parity, so all odd numbers (all primes but 2) sit in even columns; there are no straight polynomial runs.

gray.explained: The last bit of the Gray code is the second-last bit of n − 1: primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) in even columns, ≡ 3 (mod 4) in odd ones; no straight runs.

bitrev.seen: The top half full, the bottom half empty of primes.
bitrev.explained: The last binary digit of n − 1 becomes the first: every odd number lands in the top half, and so on down the digits; no straight runs.

sacks.seen: Curved streaks, bright and dark, running out from the centre.
sacks.explained: Every streak is a quadratic: x² + d on the right, x² + x + c on the left. Over 242 of them, 15,388 primes against 15,431 predicted by Bateman–Horn (correlation 0.998); the 69 with constant 0 (they factor, or all values are even) hold 0 primes. Euler’s x² + x + 41: 424 primes against 424.3.
sacks.numbers: Left streaks with even c are all even, so the left side alternates bright and dark; the right side does not.

sunflower.explained: Neighbouring seeds differ by Fibonacci numbers, so the arms are remainder classes mod 610 or 987 in the middle and 1597 or 2584 at the edge. When the Fibonacci number is even, the arms of even remainders hold no primes, so the primes fill every second arm.
sunflower.exponents: Exponents: no Fibonacci modulus from 21 to 2584 concentrates them (each p ≥ 0.16; family-wise 0.58).

theodorus.explained: The turns of Theodorus’ spiral do not line up with any arithmetic progression, so there are no arms: the rings are about π apart, and the primes thin out as 1/ln n.
theodorus.numbers: Strength of the large-scale pattern: 0.433 against 0.435 predicted from 1/ln n alone.

polar.seen: Spiral arms outside, a solid disc inside.
polar.explained: n sits at angle n radians: 44 radians is just short of 7 turns and 710 radians very nearly 113, so numbers 44 (and further out 710) apart line up on arms. Only the remainders that share no factor with the modulus hold primes: 20 of the 44 arms, 280 of the 710 (Dirichlet). The disc is where the 710 arms are closer than a pixel.
polar.numbers: Measured against predicted strengths of the arm patterns: 0.976 / 0.977 (period 2), 0.249 / 0.250 (period 10), 0.72 / 0.73 (the 44 arms).
polar.exponents: Exponents: the 31 shown cluster around one angle (mean −9°; p = 0.003 in this layout, 0.12 after the 12 round layouts). This is the earlier near-miss "cos k large" again; it does not carry over: the 21 exponents above 500,000 show no clustering at all (Rayleigh 0.18), and in 401 exponents of 79 related families the rate is 0.99. Chance.

wheel.explained: Spoke c holds the numbers ≡ c (mod 708). The 232 spokes coprime to 708 hold all primes but 2, 3 and 59; the rest hold none (Dirichlet).
wheel.numbers: Strengths of the spoke pattern: 0.999 / 1 (period 2), 0.499 / 0.5 (periods 3 and 6), all others below 0.022 (noise). Primes per spoke: 163 to 204, a little tighter than random.
wheel.exponents: Exponents: no spoke or angle stands out (family-wise p = 0.58).

binring.seen: One ring per bit length; fine stripes.
binring.explained: These four layouts carry the same data: the bit length of n and its place inside it. The only patterns are at the scale of single dots: odd and even alternate (strength 1.00), and thirds and sixths show the remainders mod 3 (0.41–0.50 against 0.413–0.5 predicted). The large scale is the plain 1/ln n thinning (0.099 / 0.100).
binring.numbers: The Mersenne numbers 2^b − 1 end every ring.
binring.exponents: Exponents: 13 of 31 sit in the first quarter of their ring (8.6 expected, p = 0.048); most of that is the log-uniform spread that random sets share; family-wise about 0.26.

decrings.seen: Six rings; the outer one partly filled.
decrings.explained: One ring per number of decimal digits; inside a ring only the dot-scale patterns of odd/even and mod 3 show.

ternrings.explained: One ring per number of base-3 digits; the same dot-scale patterns as the decimal rings.

binsquares.seen: One square per bit length; fine stripes.
binsquares.explained: These four layouts carry the same data: the bit length of n and its place inside it. The only patterns are at the scale of single dots: odd and even alternate (strength 1.00), and thirds and sixths show the remainders mod 3 (0.41–0.50 against 0.413–0.5 predicted). The large scale is the plain 1/ln n thinning (0.099 / 0.100).
binsquares.numbers: The Mersenne numbers 2^b − 1 end every square.
binsquares.exponents: Exponents: 13 of 31 sit in the first quarter of their square (8.6 expected, p = 0.048); most of that is the log-uniform spread that random sets share; family-wise about 0.26.

doubling.seen: One turn per doubling; denser outward.
doubling.explained: The angle is the fractional part of log₂ n, so every power of 2 is on one ray; the primes follow the plain 1/ln n thinning.
doubling.exponents: Exponents: 11 of 31 in the first quarter turn after a power of 2, 8.0 expected (p = 0.12; family-wise 0.56).

bintri.seen: One rows of the triangle per bit length; fine stripes.
bintri.explained: These four layouts carry the same data: the bit length of n and its place inside it. The only patterns are at the scale of single dots: odd and even alternate (strength 1.00), and thirds and sixths show the remainders mod 3 (0.41–0.50 against 0.413–0.5 predicted). The large scale is the plain 1/ln n thinning (0.099 / 0.100).
bintri.numbers: The Mersenne numbers 2^b − 1 end every row.
bintri.exponents: Exponents: 13 of 31 sit in the first quarter of their row (8.6 expected, p = 0.048); most of that is the log-uniform spread that random sets share; family-wise about 0.26.

btree.seen: One rows of the tree per bit length; fine stripes.
btree.explained: These four layouts carry the same data: the bit length of n and its place inside it. The only patterns are at the scale of single dots: odd and even alternate (strength 1.00), and thirds and sixths show the remainders mod 3 (0.41–0.50 against 0.413–0.5 predicted). The large scale is the plain 1/ln n thinning (0.099 / 0.100).
btree.numbers: The Mersenne numbers 2^b − 1 end every row.
btree.exponents: Exponents: 13 of 31 sit in the first quarter of their row (8.6 expected, p = 0.048); most of that is the log-uniform spread that random sets share; family-wise about 0.26.

omega.seen: Horizontal rows of very different lengths; row 1 is the primes.
omega.explained: Row k holds the numbers with k prime factors counted with multiplicity. Row 3 is the fullest (126,262), as Landau’s formula says at the peak (126,256); in the tails the formula is off, because large k needs many factors 2: an exact identity makes those rows halve one by one.
omega.numbers: Rows: 41,538 primes, 108,326 with two factors, 126,262 with three, 97,670 with four, …
omega.exponents: Every exponent is a prime, so all sit in row 1: the layout says nothing about them beyond that.

sieverows.seen: Rows that shrink: half of all numbers in the first, a sixth in the second, …
sieverows.explained: Row p holds the numbers whose smallest prime factor is p. Each count equals Legendre’s sieve formula exactly, and the densities are within 0.11% of (1/p)·∏(1 − 1/q) over the primes q < p. The last row is the primes from 37 on, which the sieve leaves standing.
sieverows.exponents: All exponents from 37 on sit in the last row: they are primes.

ruler.seen: A thin pyramid: each row half as long as the one above.
ruler.explained: Row k holds the numbers divisible by exactly 2^k, ⌊N/2^k⌋ − ⌊N/2^(k+1)⌋ of them (proved), so the rows halve. Every prime but 2 is odd and sits in the top row.
ruler.numbers: 250,000 numbers in row 0, 125,000 in row 1, 62,500 in row 2, …
ruler.exponents: Every exponent but 2 is in row 0, because it is odd.

turtle.seen: A tangled path that wanders off.
turtle.explained: The turtle steps once per number and turns left at every prime, so its straight runs are exactly the prime gaps and it makes a full turn every four primes. One real feature: it closes 255 small rectangles (five consecutive primes with gaps a, b, a, b) where shuffled gaps give 362 ± 21. Patterns that five primes cannot have, like 6, 6, 6, 6 (one of p, p + 6, …, p + 24 is a multiple of 5), occur 0 times; the allowed ones, most often 10, 2, 10, 2 and 2, 4, 2, 4, occur about three times as often as shuffled gaps give: the Hardy–Littlewood constants for prime patterns.
turtle.numbers: 255 rectangles, recounted from the gaps; it ends at (922, −867), an ordinary distance for shuffled gaps (35th percentile).
turtle.exponents: Exponents: their distance from the start and their headings are ordinary (p = 0.26 and 0.08; family-wise 0.49).

mertens.seen: A walk that wanders in a narrow band, between −258 and +244.
mertens.explained: M(n), the running sum of the Möbius function. Its swings stay near a sixth of √n (largest 0.47·√n, at n = 2,803), far tighter than a random walk with the same steps: none of 400 random-sign walks is as tight or crosses zero as often (4,062 times). The explicit formula with 150 zeros of the zeta function reproduces the curve with correlation 0.99: M is a sum of waves in log n, one wave per zero.
mertens.numbers: M(10^k) and the number of zeros agree with the OEIS (A084237, A171910). Scaling exponent 0.49, as for √n.
mertens.exponents: Exponents: the values M(p) at the exponents are ordinary against 3,000 random sets of the same growth (p = 0.81).
mertens.short: a sum of waves from the zeta zeros

race4.seen: A walk that climbs above zero and stays there, with one tiny dip.
race4.explained: The number of primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) minus those ≡ 1 (mod 4). Up to 500,000 it is below zero only at 26,861 and 26,862 (Leech, 1957). Its average height, about 1.23·√n / ln n against 1.24 predicted, comes from the prime squares, which are all ≡ 1 (mod 4): Chebyshev’s bias. The wiggles follow the zeros of the L-function of the character mod 4 (correlation 0.93 with 64 zeros).
race4.numbers: Leader changes and ties agree with the OEIS (A007350, A007351) through 629,371.
race4.exponents: Exponents: the race height at the exponents is ordinary (p = 0.72).

liouville.seen: The walk drops below the axis and stays there.
liouville.explained: L(n), the running sum of λ(n) = (−1)^Ω(n). It touches 0 only at 2, 4, 6, 10, 16, 26, 40, 96 and 586, and is negative from there up to 1,000,000 (Pólya’s conjecture holds here; it first fails at 906,150,257). Its average level, −0.675·√n, matches 1/ζ(½) = −0.685, the pole of ζ(2s)/ζ(s) at s = ½, and the wiggles follow the zeta zeros (correlation 0.993). A random ±1 walk would cross zero hundreds of times.
liouville.numbers: The zeros of L and its sign rechecked in plain integers up to 1,000,000.
liouville.exponents: Exponents: L(p) at the exponents is ordinary (p = 0.82).
liouville.short: below zero: Pólya, the zeta zeros
